summary:
The field-experiment literature, about 300 randomized trials mostly from the US, agrees on a few points. Personal, conversational contact raises turnout. Impersonal contact (robocalls, email, digital ads, advocacy mail) does little or nothing. Effects are much smaller in high-salience national elections and outside the US. Both conditions hold for a Knesset election with roughly 70% turnout.

Mann and Haenschen re-analysed 240 experiments and found effects fall 33-62% from low- to high-salience elections. In high-salience US races they estimate: door-to-door canvassing about 3 pp per completed contact, volunteer calls about 2.3, paid calls about 0.7, cold SMS about 0.2 per targeted voter, standard mail about 0.3 per piece. In Europe, pooled canvassing is only about 0.8 pp per contact (CI -0.2 to 1.7), against 2.5 in the US. In France, canvassing did not change turnout but did shift vote share. For Israel we should therefore budget about 1-2 pp per completed door conversation with an identified supporter, about 1 pp per volunteer call, 0.2-0.6 pp per SMS, and roughly zero for robocalls, email, ads and partisan leaflets. Friend-to-friend (relational) contact is the main exception. One large trial found about 8 pp per message actually received (CI 1-15) even when baseline turnout was about 75%.

For locality targeting, how much people respond depends on how likely they already are to vote. Meta-analysis of canvassing shows the largest effects where control-group turnout is 30-50% (about 6 pp), smaller effects at 50-70% (about 1.4-2 pp), and almost none above 70%. In high-salience elections, casual and lower-propensity voters are the ones near the decision threshold. Even so, unfocused GOTV tends to mobilise the already-engaged and can widen participation gaps. So the model should score localities on the number of change-bloc supporters with mid-range turnout propensity, not on raw turnout gaps. It should also cap gains in localities that already turn out above about 80%.

Effects add up. A saturation campaign raised turnout about 7 pp in heavily targeted US states, and over 10 pp in targeted subgroups. Spillover to other household members is about 30-60% of the direct effect. There is no measurable spillover across households, so the unit to count is the household. Contacts made in the final week to ten days work best, and reminders sent before election day beat ones sent on the day. With 16 days left, almost the whole remaining campaign falls inside the GOTV window.

Persuading voters to switch is close to zero in US general elections. It was larger in France, where canvassing was novel, so persuasion should carry a small, uncertain weight.

Visible campaigning that stresses an outgroup's turnout can cause a backlash. Likud's 2019 polling-station camera campaign is widely judged to have woken up Arab voters: Arab turnout went from 49% to 59%, and a Likud MK said as much publicly. UK partisan experiments show differential mobilisation. Racial-threat studies show proximity to an outgroup raising turnout. No rigorous estimate exists for the 2015 Netanyahu 'droves' video. The practical conclusion is to keep work in opposing strongholds and mixed areas targeted and low-visibility, and to price a counter-mobilisation penalty into broadcast-style tactics.

Note: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through. Some items (TV-ad decay, Japan, Italy, Ireland, and published DOIs for Enos & Fowler and the Gerber & Green chapter) could not be checked further and were left out or flagged.

findings.topic: Tactic effect sizes by electoral salience (meta-analysis)
findings.claim: Re-analysis of 240 US GOTV experiments catalogued in Green & Gerber (2019), split by election salience. Every tactic's effect shrinks by roughly one-third to two-thirds from low- to high-salience elections. Only 40 of the 240 experiments were run in presidential cycles. Once realistic contact rates are applied, canvassing and phone banking need very high contact rates to beat cheap tactics on an intent-to-treat basis. The authors argue GOTV effect sizes are not settled science and should be planned with salience-specific numbers.
findings.quant: High-salience (low-salience) estimates. CACE: canvassing 3.05 pp [1.20, 4.90], n=24 (4.58 [2.97, 6.18]); volunteer phone 2.28 [1.12, 3.43] (3.62); paid phone 0.74 [0.31, 1.17] (1.66). ITT: social-pressure mail 1.38 [0.31, 2.45] (2.45); standard mail 0.28 [0.13, 0.43] (0.46), and 0.05 [-0.24, 0.33] in presidential cycles; warm SMS 0.68 [0.05, 1.41]; cold SMS 0.22 [0.05, 0.39] (0.58); robocalls 0.58 at low salience only. Attenuation 33-62% by tactic. Typical contact rates: canvass 25-30%, volunteer phones 10-12%, professional phones about 6% (2018).
findings.authors: Christopher B. Mann; Katherine Haenschen
findings.title: A meta-analysis of voter mobilization tactics by electoral salience
findings.venue: Electoral Studies 87, 102729 (doi:10.1016/j.electstud.2023.102729); numbers read from the authors' republication on VoteAmerica Research
findings.relevance: Primary calibration source for per-contact effects. A Knesset election is high-salience, so use the high-salience column as the US ceiling and apply a further non-US discount (see D3-F24). Use the contact rates to turn per-contact effects into effects per attempted target.

findings.topic: Canonical meta-analysis of GOTV tactics
findings.claim: Green, McGrath and Aronow pooled every field experiment with validated turnout they could find (about 294 studies in the replication archive). Personal contact clearly beats impersonal contact. Door-to-door canvassing has the largest per-contact effect, then volunteer phone calls, then commercial calls. Conventional leaflets and mail have tiny effects, and partisan leaflets and mail show no positive effect. Averaged over everyone targeted rather than everyone reached, the effects are about 1 pp for canvassing, 0.7 for mail and 0.4 for phones.
findings.quant: CACE: canvassing 2.536 pp [1.817, 3.255], 71 studies; volunteer calls 1.936 [1.298, 2.575], 37; commercial calls 0.980 [0.504, 1.456], 25. ITT: conventional leaflets/mail 0.162 [0.078, 0.247], 110; partisan leaflets/mail -0.213 (n.s.). Overall ITT averages (via Enos & Fowler): canvass 1.0, mail 0.7, phone 0.4.
findings.authors: Donald P. Green; Mary C. McGrath; Peter M. Aronow
findings.title: Field Experiments and the Study of Voter Turnout
findings.venue: Journal of Elections, Public Opinion & Parties 23(1): 27-48 (doi:10.1080/17457289.2012.728223)
findings.relevance: Baseline ordering of tactics and the all-election average. Most of these studies were low-salience US elections, so the figures should be treated as upper bounds for Israel. Tactic-level numbers were verified through Table 1 of Townsley (D3-F27) and through Bhatti et al. (D3-F24).

findings.topic: Canvassing effect by baseline (control-group) turnout
findings.claim: A random-effects meta-analysis of US canvassing experiments, grouped by control-group turnout, finds a hump-shaped pattern. Effects are large in low- and moderate-turnout settings, biggest at 30-50% turnout, much smaller at 50-70%, and statistically indistinguishable from zero at 70% and above.
findings.quant: Average CACE, all canvassing: under 30% turnout, 4.6 pp [2.4, 6.9]; 30-50%, 6.2 [4.2, 8.2]; 50-70%, 1.4 [-1.2, 4.0]; 70% and above, 0.6 [-1.5, 2.8]. Non-advocacy canvassing only: 3.3 / 6.7 / 2.1 [0.1, 4.1] / 0.6.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Donald P. Green
findings.year: 2014 (draft); later a Handbook of Economic Field Experiments chapter
findings.title: Field Experiments on Voter Mobilization: An Overview of a Burgeoning Literature
findings.venue: NBER conference draft (later published in Handbook of Economic Field Experiments vol. 1, Elsevier; chapter DOI not verified)
findings.relevance: Use this to build a responsiveness curve for each locality and voter segment: weight targets whose baseline propensity is 30-60% most heavily and down-weight localities above 75-80%. Bhatti et al. (D3-F24) find the relationship weaker and only marginally significant once European data are added, so apply it as a soft multiplier.

findings.topic: Direct mail and leaflets (meta-analysis)
findings.claim: Pooled US direct-mail experiments, 1998-2014. Advocacy mail (pushing a candidate or issue) has essentially zero turnout effect. Non-advocacy GOTV mail has a small positive effect. Mail using social pressure is several times stronger. Earlier experiments show diminishing returns after about six pieces per household. Mail aimed at ethnic-minority communities was mostly ineffective.
findings.quant: Random-effects ITT per piece: advocacy 0.010 pp [-0.101, 0.120], 19 studies; non-advocacy 0.523 [0.299, 0.748], 51 (0.366 without gratitude/norm mailers); social pressure 2.280 [1.259, 3.301], 15; all mail 0.759 [0.530, 0.988], 85. New Haven 1998: +0.5 pp per additional mailer. Minority-targeted mail: 19 of 38 experiments had positive estimates.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Donald P. Green
findings.title: Field Experiments on Voter Mobilization: An Overview of a Burgeoning Literature (Handbook chapter draft)
findings.venue: J-PAL hosted draft of Handbook of Economic Field Experiments chapter
findings.relevance: Set party leaflets and advocacy mail to roughly zero turnout effect. Mail or flyers with GOTV wording get a small per-piece effect; Mann & Haenschen (D3-F01) put it at 0.28 pp in high-salience elections. Do not rank localities by how much material is distributed there.

findings.topic: Social-pressure messaging and backlash
findings.claim: In the 2006 Michigan primary experiment (about 180,000 households, one mailer sent 11 days before), turnout rose with the strength of social pressure. Replications of the 'Self' mailer, which showed a household's own vote history, give 4-36% relative gains, with the strongest effects in low-salience races and weaker, non-significant effects in high-turnout general elections. A partisan version of the Self mailer had no effect. Some recipients reacted against the mailers, but Mann (2010) found gentler versions designed to reduce that reaction worked just as well. Gratitude mailers that thank people for past voting gave about 2.4-2.5 pp. The effects persisted into later elections.
findings.quant: Control turnout 29.7%. Civic duty +1.8 pp, Self +4.9 pp, Neighbors +8.1 pp. Self replications: TX 2010 general +2.6 pp, WI 2010 +1.8 pp (both n.s.). Gratitude mailers about 2.4-2.5 pp. The Self mailer produced about 1,850 votes in 2006 plus about 900 more over the next three August primaries.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Donald P. Green; Christopher W. Larimer (replications summarised by Gerber & Green; Mann 2010 on reactance)
findings.title: Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
findings.relevance: Message design: descriptive norms, gratitude and accountability framing add effect. The partisan version did not work, and Israeli parties may not be able to use individual vote histories legally or practically, so for change-bloc material use gentle non-partisan norm or gratitude framing at about 0.5 pp rather than 2-8 pp.

findings.topic: Volunteer phone banks and cost per vote
findings.claim: Eight volunteer, non-partisan phone campaigns in six US cities (2000-01) raised turnout among people reached. That contradicts the earlier null result for professional phone banks, and the author attributes the difference to call quality and personal tone. At volunteer-equivalent wages, cost per vote was competitive with canvassing.
findings.quant: +3.8 pp among those contacted; about $26 per vote (at $15/hour). Comparisons from the earlier Green-Gerber data: canvassing about $32 per vote, leaflets $23-47, direct mail $69. Professional calls in New Haven/West Haven pooled -1.6 pp (n.s.).
findings.authors: David W. Nickerson
findings.title: Volunteer Phone Calls Can Increase Turnout: Evidence From Eight Field Experiments
findings.relevance: Supports a meaningful but discounted volunteer-call parameter (about 1 pp per completed call for Israel after salience and non-US discounts) and sets relative cost-per-vote references. The dollar figures are old US numbers and should be re-costed for Israeli volunteer and staff time.

findings.topic: Commercial calls: quality, scripts and final-week timing
findings.claim: Large commercial phone-bank experiments find very small effects. The per-vote figures below are how many completed calls it took to generate one extra vote. A longer, chattier script helped, and high-quality vendors beat low-quality ones. Unusually good calls to young voters raised turnout only when made in the final week; calls in the first three weeks of a month-long drive had no detectable effect.
findings.quant: 2002 nonpartisan: 1 vote per about 280 contacts (about 0.36 pp). 2004 Illinois: 1 per 55. Ha & Karlan (NC/MO): 1 per 500. Standard script 1.2 pp vs chatty script 3.4 pp (1 per 30). Mann & Klofstad (2010): low-quality vendors 0.2 pp vs high-quality 0.9-1.4 pp. Nickerson (2007): final-week calls 1 vote per 20 contacts (about 5 pp); earlier calls about 0.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Donald P. Green (reviewing Nickerson 2007; Ha & Karlan; Mann & Klofstad 2015)
findings.title: Field Experiments on Voter Mobilization: An Overview of a Burgeoning Literature (Handbook chapter draft)
findings.relevance: Use as a timing weight: put live GOTV contact in the last 7-10 days, i.e. from about 17-27 Oct 2026. Paid call centres should get a small parameter (about 0.3 pp) that depends on vendor quality, and conversational scripts should be required.

findings.topic: Text messages: noticeable reminders and heterogeneity
findings.claim: Dale & Strauss (2009) found a text reminder sent to newly registered voters in 2006 raised turnout by 3 pp, which led to the 'noticeable reminder' theory: a salient but impersonal reminder can be enough. Malhotra et al. replicated this with cold texts (no prior relationship) in San Mateo County and found a smaller average effect. The effect depended on election salience and voting history. In a sleepy local election only habitual voters responded. In a higher-salience statewide primary only casual voters responded, and habitual voters did not.
findings.quant: Dale & Strauss ITT 3.0 pp (N=8,053, warm texts to new registrants). Cold texts 0.7-0.9 pp average. Low salience: habitual voters +16.2 pp, others about 0. Higher salience: presidential-only voters +1.0 pp (s.e. 0.4), major-election voters +2.3 pp (s.e. 0.8), habitual voters about 0. Green & Gerber 2019 meta-analysis of automated texting: 0.29 pp (cited in Schein et al.).
findings.authors: Neil Malhotra; Melissa R. Michelson; Todd Rogers; Ali Adam Valenzuela (replicating Allison Dale & Aaron Strauss 2009, AJPS 53(4): 787-804)
findings.title: Text Messages as Mobilization Tools: The Conditional Effect of Habitual Voting and Election Salience
findings.relevance: SMS is cheap and scalable but small per message: about 0.2-0.3 pp cold, 0.5-0.7 pp warm. In a high-salience Knesset race, aim it at casual and occasional supporters, not habitual voters. Most useful for large lists in priority localities in the final days.

findings.topic: SMS mobilisation in a European multiparty setting (Denmark)
findings.claim: Four SMS experiments with over 300,000 Danish voters around two elections (2013 municipal, 2014 European Parliament), sent by a sender the recipients had no prior relationship with. Texts raised turnout modestly. Messages sent before election day worked better than messages sent on election day. Extra messages added nothing, and message wording made no significant difference.
findings.quant: ITT 0.33 to 1.82 pp across experiments; pooled 0.74 pp. No added effect from multiple messages.
findings.authors: Yosef Bhatti; Jens Olav Dahlgaard; Jonas Hedegaard Hansen; Kasper M. Hansen
findings.title: Moving the campaign from the front door to the front pocket: field experimental evidence on the effect of phrasing and timing of text messages on voter turnout
findings.venue: Journal of Elections, Public Opinion & Parties 27(3)
findings.relevance: The best non-US PR-system estimate for SMS, though from second-order elections. Plan one or two texts in the 1-3 days before 27 Oct, not mainly on election day. Do not pay for repeated blasts to the same person.

findings.topic: Household spillover of SMS mobilisation (Denmark)
findings.claim: In two nationwide Danish SMS experiments aimed at young voters, about 30% of the direct effect appeared to spill over to other members of the same household. Spillover to parents living elsewhere was essentially zero. The authors note the spillover is hard to establish statistically because the direct effects are small.
findings.quant: Spillover about 30% of the direct effect within households. Example direct effect 1.82 pp. Spillover to parents not living with the young voter 0.02 pp.
findings.authors: Yosef Bhatti; Jens Olav Dahlgaard; Jonas Hedegaard Hansen; Kasper Møller Hansen
findings.title: How Voter Mobilization from Short Text Messages Travels within Households and Families: Evidence from Two Nationwide Field Experiments
findings.relevance: Household multiplier of about 0.3 for impersonal contact (versus about 0.6 for canvassing, D3-F14). Living together, not family ties, is what carries the effect.

findings.topic: Email, social media and digital ads
findings.claim: Email GOTV generally does nothing: one partisan election-eve and election-day email programme found slightly lower turnout in the treatment group. On Facebook, an 'it's election day' banner alone had zero effect; adding faces of friends who had voted gave a small, significant gain. That feature is not something campaigns can buy. Two large purchased Facebook-ad experiments (Rock the Vote) found no effect on turnout.
findings.quant: Email (NYC 2005 DNC): treatment 58.7% vs control 59.7%. Bond et al. 2012 (61 million users): information banner 0 pp; social banner +0.39 pp. Rock the Vote FB ads 2012: 56.5% vs 56.5%; 2013: 14.0% vs 14.6%.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Donald P. Green (reviewing Stollwerk; Bond et al. 2012, Nature 489: 295-298; Collins, Keane & Kalla 2014)
findings.title: Field Experiments on Voter Mobilization: An Overview of a Burgeoning Literature (Handbook chapter draft)
findings.relevance: Set the turnout effect of email and paid digital ads to about 0 in the allocation model. Digital spending can be justified for other goals such as recruiting volunteers or relational organisers, not for direct turnout. Social-proof content shared between people who know each other is the exception.

findings.topic: Relational (friend-to-friend) organising
findings.claim: A randomised element in the Outvote app (2018 US midterms) let the authors estimate the effect of users texting people in their own contacts. The effect was very large for a GOTV trial even though compliers already had high baseline turnout. Fewer than a third of intended targets actually got a message. Compliers here are people who received a message only because they were assigned to the treatment group.
findings.quant: Unadjusted ITT 3.02 pp (s.e. 1.10), CACE 11.88. Covariate-adjusted ITT 2.09 pp (s.e. 0.91), CACE 8.26 pp [1.18, 15.34]. Turnout around 76-79%. For comparison, the Green & Gerber 2019 meta estimate for automated texts is 0.29 pp.
findings.authors: Aaron Schein; Keyon Vafa; Dhanya Sridhar; Victor Veitch; Jeffrey Quinn; James Moffet; David M. Blei; Donald P. Green
findings.title: A Digital Field Experiment Reveals Large Effects of Friend-to-Friend Texting on Voter Turnout
findings.venue: Working paper (Columbia University); also hosted at MIT Media Lab
findings.relevance: The strongest evidence that personal ties matter even when turnout is high, which suits Israel's dense family and community networks. Model relational contact at about 3 pp per completed contact, discounted from 8.3 because this is a single study with a wide CI. Recruiting and equipping supporters to contact friends in target localities should be a priority line in the plan.

findings.topic: Election-day festivals and events at polling places
findings.claim: Fourteen randomised experiments with non-partisan election-day festivals at polling places (food, music, family-friendly; 2005-06 US local elections) raised turnout at the precinct level. The effect depended on baseline turnout, and cost per vote was competitive.
findings.quant: Estimated +6.5 pp where expected baseline is 50%; +2.6 pp at a 10% baseline; about $28 per vote. The first event (Hooksett, NH) gave +2-3 pp.
findings.authors: Elizabeth M. Addonizio; Donald P. Green; James M. Glaser (summarised by CIRCLE)
findings.title: Putting the Party Back into Politics: An Experiment Testing Whether Election Day Festivals Increase Voter Turnout
findings.relevance: A possible polling-station-level tactic in priority neighbourhoods, since election day is a public holiday in Israel. Must comply with Israeli election-propaganda rules near polling stations. These were low-salience US elections, so use about 1.5 pp at the polling-station level (range 0-4).

findings.topic: Implementation intentions / vote-plan scripts
findings.claim: In a phone experiment before the 2008 Pennsylvania Democratic presidential primary, lower-propensity Democrats (at most one primary vote since 2000) who were asked to make a concrete voting plan (when, from where, what they'd be doing beforehand) turned out more. A standard GOTV call and a 'will you vote?' self-prediction call had no significant effect. The whole effect came from single-voter households. Later replications are mixed: a mailer version gave about 0.5 pp, and one phone replication was null.
findings.quant: N=287,228; contact rate about 23-26%. ITT: standard -0.1 pp, self-prediction +0.5, plan-making +0.9 (s.e. 0.4). Effect among contacted: standard -0.2, self-prediction 2.0, plan-making 4.1 pp (s.e. 1.7). Single-voter households 9.1 pp; multi-voter households about 0.
findings.authors: David W. Nickerson; Todd Rogers
findings.title: Do You Have a Voting Plan? Implementation Intentions, Voter Turnout, and Organic Plan Making
findings.relevance: Add a vote-plan module to every live contact script: when, which polling station, who you're going with. Model it as about +1 pp on top of the live-contact effect, larger for single-voter households such as young singles and the elderly living alone.

findings.topic: Household contagion of canvassing effects
findings.claim: A placebo-controlled canvassing study in two-voter households (Denver and Minneapolis, 2002 primaries) measured the turnout of the household member who did not answer the door. About 60% of the effect on the person contacted carried over to that second household member.
findings.quant: Spillover about 60% of the direct effect within two-voter households, in both experiments.
findings.authors: David W. Nickerson
findings.title: Is Voting Contagious? Evidence from Two Field Experiments
findings.relevance: Household multiplier for face-to-face contact. Each completed doorstep conversation yields about 1 + 0.6 x (other eligible voters in the household) units of effect. This makes multi-voter households of supporters more valuable door targets and favours dense residential areas.

findings.topic: No spillover across households / neighbourhoods
findings.claim: A multilevel experiment in Chicago (April 2009 special election, about 64,000 people) varied how many households in a postcode block got social-pressure mail: all, half or none. Treatment effects were positive and there was some spillover within households, but no detectable spillover to neighbouring households.
findings.quant: Within-household spillover: some evidence. Across households: no detectable effect.
findings.authors: Betsy Sinclair; Margaret McConnell; Donald P. Green
findings.title: Detecting Spillover Effects: Design and Analysis of Multilevel Experiments
findings.relevance: Don't count neighbourhood contagion when allocating contacts within a locality. Locality-level effects should equal the sum of direct and household effects. Saturating a neighbourhood does not create extra returns from contagion.

findings.topic: Partisan disagreement and spillover in households (UK)
findings.claim: A UK spillover experiment combining pre-treatment party-preference data with official turnout records. Mobilisation spread more within politically mixed households than within like-minded ones, and more when the message was more strongly partisan. The authors read this as evidence that political discussion, not simple imitation, carries the effect.
findings.quant: Larger spillover in mixed-party households, increasing with partisan intensity (no specific magnitudes extracted).
findings.authors: Florian Foos; Eline A. de Rooij
findings.title: All in the Family: Partisan Disagreement and Electoral Mobilization in Intimate Networks - A Spillover Experiment
findings.relevance: Strongly partisan GOTV at the door can also mobilise household members who back other parties. In mixed-bloc localities, use bloc-neutral turnout framing at the door or target confirmed supporter households, to limit mobilising Netanyahu-bloc members of the same household.

findings.topic: Who is mobilised: propensity and salience
findings.claim: A re-analysis of 11 face-to-face GOTV experiments supports a threshold model. Contact moves only people close to the point of indifference between voting and abstaining, and where that point sits depends on the election's salience. In high-profile elections, low-propensity citizens are the ones near it; in quiet elections it is high-propensity citizens.
findings.quant: Qualitative pattern across 11 experiments. An informal reading is: target rare voters in high-visibility elections, regular voters in obscure ones, occasional voters in between.
findings.authors: Kevin Arceneaux; David W. Nickerson
findings.title: Who Is Mobilized to Vote? A Re-Analysis of 11 Field Experiments
findings.relevance: A Knesset election is high-salience, so the best targets are supporters with low-to-middle predicted propensity, not habitual voters. At locality level, give more weight to localities with many supporters who vote only some of the time.

findings.topic: GOTV can widen participation gaps
findings.claim: Pooling data on about 1.2 million people from GOTV experiments, the authors find that high-propensity groups respond more to standard mobilisation. GOTV therefore tends to widen turnout inequality, drawing in more educated, higher-income citizens and those with more extreme views.
findings.quant: Treatment effects increase with the group's predicted propensity to vote (no single number extracted).
findings.authors: Ryan D. Enos; Anthony Fowler; Lynn Vavreck
findings.title: Increasing Inequality: The Effect of GOTV Mobilization on the Composition of the Electorate
findings.relevance: A warning against assuming that low-turnout localities give the biggest returns. Without tailored, personal, in-community contact (D3-F20), effort put into low-propensity areas is used inefficiently. Model responsiveness as rising with propensity at low levels and falling at the top.

findings.topic: Mobilising low-propensity ethnic and minority communities
findings.claim: Drawing on 268 GOTV experiments run with community groups in California between 2006 and 2008, the authors find low-propensity voters in ethnic-minority communities can be mobilised. It takes well-organised personal contact, door-to-door or live phone, ideally by messengers from the voter's own community and in their language, with follow-up contacts. Mail and voter guides were weak.
findings.quant: 268 experiments; follow-up phone contacts reported up to about 10 pp in summaries; mail mostly null (19 of 38 positive, per Gerber & Green).
findings.authors: Lisa García Bedolla; Melissa R. Michelson
findings.title: Mobilizing Inclusion: Transforming the Electorate through Get-Out-the-Vote Campaigns
findings.relevance: Relevant to lower-turnout segments such as Russian-speaking, Ethiopian-Israeli, Druze, Bedouin, periphery and young voters. Messenger matching and in-language contact should raise the effect multiplier. Impersonal outreach to these groups should be treated as near zero.

findings.topic: Aggregate effect of a saturation ground campaign
findings.claim: Comparing battleground and non-battleground states within the same media markets in 2012, using records on all eligible voters and internal campaign contact data, the authors estimate that the full presidential ground campaign raised turnout substantially. Effects of multiple contacts were roughly additive. Gains were largest among predicted partisans the campaigns targeted, and TV and online ads contributed little.
findings.quant: About +7 pp aggregate turnout in the most heavily targeted states; more than +10 pp in targeted subgroups; about 2.6 million additional voters. Romney campaign alone made about 225 million contact attempts.
findings.authors: Ryan D. Enos; Anthony Fowler
findings.year: 2016 (working paper version; later published in Political Science Research and Methods; DOI not verified)
findings.title: The Effects of Large-Scale Campaigns on Voter Turnout: Evidence from 400 Million Voter Contacts
findings.relevance: Justifies stacking several contacts per target in priority localities, treating effects as additive with a cap of about 8-10 pp per targeted person. Implies concentrated saturation of top localities beats spreading effort thinly.

findings.topic: Door-to-door canvassing in Europe (meta-study)
findings.claim: Pooling nine European canvassing experiments (UK, Spain, France, Sweden, Italy and two new Danish studies) gives an effect well below the US average and not distinguishable from zero. Both Danish experiments found nothing. The largest European effect came from the only first-past-the-post election. Baseline turnout explains little of the gap. Volunteers worked in Italy but candidates did not.
findings.quant: European pooled CACE 0.78 pp [-0.16, 1.71] vs US 2.50 [1.77, 3.22]. Studies: John & Brannan UK 6.7 (s.e. 3.7); Pons & Liegey FR 0.4 (0.8); Pons FR 0.5 (0.7); Nyman SE 3.6 (1.9); Foos & John UK -8.5 (4.3); Cantoni & Pons IT volunteers 5.0 (2.2) vs candidates -0.4 (2.6); Copenhagen -2.1 (4.6); Randers -15.4 (13.9).
findings.authors: Yosef Bhatti; Jens Olav Dahlgaard; Jonas Hedegaard Hansen; Kasper M. Hansen
findings.title: Is Door-to-Door Canvassing Effective in Europe? Evidence from a Meta-study across Six European Countries
findings.relevance: The main reason to discount US canvassing effects for Israel, which has PR, high turnout and multiparty competition. Use about 0.5 times US high-salience effects for canvassing, with wide uncertainty. Volunteers rather than candidates should knock on doors.

findings.topic: UK nonpartisan canvassing vs telephoning
findings.claim: A non-partisan GOTV experiment in one constituency at the 2005 British general election found that both canvassing and telephoning raised turnout. The authors attribute the impact to the personal, face-to-face nature of the contact rather than to message content or information. Later UK work suggests volunteer phone banks work especially well there.
findings.quant: Canvassing ITT 3.6 pp, CACE 6.7 pp (s.e. 3.7); N=2,510; contact rate 54%; control turnout 46.3% (via Bhatti et al. Table 1).
findings.authors: Peter John; Tessa Brannan
findings.title: How Different Are Telephoning and Canvassing? Results from a 'Get Out the Vote' Field Experiment in the British 2005 General Election
findings.relevance: Shows personal contact can work in a national parliamentary election outside the US, though with a small sample and wide CI. Supports keeping a positive canvassing and phone parameter for Israel rather than zero.

findings.topic: Impersonal methods in a nationwide English experiment
findings.claim: A large, nationally representative two-wave GOTV experiment in England found that impersonal methods (phone and direct mail) worked better than earlier studies suggested, with the size depending on context. Effects built up within and across elections with repeated contact, and adding methods together produced no extra synergy.
findings.quant: Cumulative, additive effects of repeated contacts; no synergy (magnitudes not extracted from the abstract).
findings.authors: Edward Fieldhouse; David Cutts; Paul Widdop; Peter John
findings.title: Do impersonal mobilisation methods work? Evidence from a nationwide Get-Out-the-Vote experiment in England
findings.relevance: Mail and phone can work where people receive less junk contact. Israeli voters are heavily bombarded with robocalls and SMS at election time, which probably pushes effects toward the low end. Supports additive modelling of multiple contacts (D3-F21).

findings.topic: Partisan campaigning in Europe; differential mobilisation
findings.claim: A partisan experiment with the Liberal Democrats at the 2017 English local elections, in an unfavourable area, found party leaflets raised turnout and a canvass visit added little on top. The paper also reviews European partisan experiments. Partisan phone calls added 2-3 pp in the UK (Foos & de Rooij), canvassing added 3.6 pp in Sweden (Nyman), and party contact randomised at aggregate level often shows nulls. There is emerging evidence of 'differential mobilisation': partisan campaigns mobilise their own supporters while demobilising rival supporters (Foos & John 2016).
findings.quant: Leaflets +4.3 pp (among in-person voters); leaflet plus canvass +4.9 pp; extra effect of the canvass +0.6 pp (n.s.); any campaign contact +3.6 pp. N=6,525.
findings.authors: Joshua Townsley
findings.title: Is it worth door-knocking? Evidence from a United Kingdom-based Get Out The Vote (GOTV) field experiment on the effect of party leaflets and canvass visits on voter turnout
findings.relevance: In multiparty systems partisan contact can work, but it can also demobilise rivals. For a bloc campaign, partisan contact in swing localities might lower Netanyahu-bloc turnout among mixed audiences, but that could reverse if the contact is seen as provocative (D3-F31/F32). The 4.3 pp leaflet result is an outlier compared with US mail and comes from a low-salience local election.

findings.topic: Persuasion vs turnout in France (multiparty, countrywide)
findings.claim: Hollande's 2012 campaign knocked on about 5 million doors, randomised by precinct across 4,674 precincts (about 5 million registered voters). Canvassing did not change turnout but raised Hollande's vote share, and the effect lasted into later elections. The author suggests novelty mattered, since most voters had never been canvassed before.
findings.quant: Turnout effect: none significant. Vote share +3.2 pp in round 1 and +2.8 pp in round 2 in treated precincts. Accounts for about half of Hollande's first-round lead and a quarter of his second-round margin.
findings.authors: Vincent Pons
findings.title: Will a Five-Minute Discussion Change Your Mind? A Countrywide Experiment on Voter Choice in France
findings.relevance: In a multiparty European system, door-to-door contact may move vote choice more than turnout. Canvassing in swing localities should be credited with a persuasion effect, small and uncertain. The Pons design (randomising by precinct and measuring with official results) is directly usable with Israeli polling-station results to evaluate this campaign.

findings.topic: Minimal persuasion in general elections
findings.claim: A meta-analysis of 40 field experiments plus 9 new ones finds the best estimate of campaign contact and advertising effects on candidate choice in US general elections is zero. Exceptions: when a candidate takes unusually unpopular positions and the campaign invests heavily in finding persuadable voters; and when contact comes long before election day and is measured immediately, but that early persuasion decays.
findings.quant: Average persuasion effect in general elections about 0 (40 prior + 9 original experiments).
findings.authors: Joshua L. Kalla; David E. Broockman
findings.title: The Minimal Persuasive Effects of Campaign Contact in General Elections: Evidence from 49 Field Experiments
findings.relevance: Together with Pons, this argues for a small default persuasion weight. Sixteen days out, campaign resources should go mostly to mobilising identified supporters rather than converting voters across blocs, except for carefully identified cross-pressured voters.

findings.topic: Door-to-door mobilisation in a low-turnout, low-information setting (Pakistan)
findings.claim: In rural Pakistan, a door-to-door campaign explaining why voting matters and how voting works raised women's turnout. Untreated women in treated clusters gained about as much as targeted women, showing large information spillovers through women's networks. Treated women were also more likely to vote independently of their household's choice.
findings.quant: About +11 pp turnout for women in treated clusters (both targeted and untargeted). Treating 10 women produced about 7 extra votes; about $3.1 per vote. A 10% increase in the share of treated women at a polling station cut the winning party's share by 7%. Working-paper version: 12 pp and $2.3 per vote.
findings.authors: Xavier Giné; Ghazala Mansuri
findings.title: Together We Will: Experimental Evidence on Female Voting Behavior in Pakistan
findings.relevance: In low-information, low-turnout, tightly networked communities, practical polling-station information spread through peer networks can produce large effects and spillovers. It is an imperfect analogy for some Israeli groups with low turnout and closed networks.

findings.topic: Timing of GOTV contact
findings.claim: A randomised experiment in Rochester, NY (2005 municipal election) compared non-partisan commercial calls placed 4 weeks, 2 weeks and 3 days before election day. It found that early calls can also work in a low-salience election, which qualifies Nickerson's (2007) finding that only final-week calls matter.
findings.quant: About 25,000 registered voters. Calls at 4 weeks, 2 weeks and 3 days out. Early calls also effective (effect sizes not extracted).
findings.authors: Costas Panagopoulos
findings.title: Timing Is Everything? Primacy and Recency Effects in Voter Mobilization Campaigns
findings.relevance: Early contact may matter more in low-salience races, where it alerts people that an election is coming. In a high-salience Knesset race everyone knows the election is on, so weight the evidence toward recency (D3-F07, D3-F09). Concentrate GOTV in the final 7-10 days, with a reminder 1-3 days out.

findings.topic: Persistence: voting is habit-forming
findings.claim: Using random encouragements to vote and 18th-birthday eligibility cutoffs, the authors estimate that voting in one election raises the chance of voting in a later one by about 10 pp on average. The size varies with election type and timing and with who was induced to vote. GOTV effects therefore partly carry into future elections.
findings.quant: About +10 pp future turnout from voting once (average; varies by context).
findings.authors: Alexander Coppock; Donald P. Green
findings.title: Is Voting Habit Forming? New Evidence from Experiments and Regression Discontinuities
findings.relevance: Secondary for a 16-day horizon. It means mobilising first-time and young voters in 2026 builds a habit that pays off in later elections, which is relevant if early elections or repeat rounds follow a deadlock (about 60% probability in the 10 Oct forecast).

findings.topic: Outgroup proximity and turnout (racial threat)
findings.claim: When Chicago demolished public housing (2000-04), more than 25,000 African Americans were displaced. White voters who had lived nearby then voted less, and the drop shrank with distance from the projects. Proximity was also linked to more conservative voting. The author reads this as evidence that a nearby, visible outgroup mobilises majority-group voters. The article has faced research-integrity critiques, which should be read alongside it.
findings.quant: White turnout fell by more than 10 pp after removal. About -13.4 pp nearest the projects, about -10.7 pp further out; effects still about 15 pp within 500 m in some specifications.
findings.authors: Ryan D. Enos
findings.title: What the Demolition of Public Housing Teaches Us about the Impact of Racial Threat on Political Behavior
findings.relevance: Theoretical basis for a counter-mobilisation penalty. Making an outgroup's turnout salient, as with Arab or Haredi turnout narratives, can mobilise the other side. Keep messaging about other groups' turnout out of public, broadcast channels.

findings.topic: Israel: backlash from Likud's 2019 anti-Arab-turnout campaign
findings.claim: Likud placed cameras in Arab polling stations in April 2019, pushed a 'camera bill' and ran a campaign warning about Arab turnout ahead of September 2019. Analysts and a senior Likud MK concluded it backfired and woke up Arab voters. Arab turnout rose sharply between the two 2019 elections. The Joint List's reunification is a confound that has not been separated out.
findings.quant: Arab turnout 49% (April 2019, a record low) to 59% (September 2019), per IDI's Arik Rudnitzky. Joint List seats 10 to 13. Likud MK Miki Zohar, paraphrased: the camera push woke the Arab sector and lulled right-wing voters into complacency.
findings.authors: NBC News (citing Israel Democracy Institute data)
findings.title: How Netanyahu's campaign against Israel's Arab citizens backfired
findings.relevance: Israel-specific evidence that visible group-threat campaigning can backfire. For the change bloc, avoid high-visibility activity in or about Netanyahu-bloc strongholds that could revive a 'threat' narrative. Expect the Netanyahu bloc's late campaign to use this kind of threat framing, and prepare a quiet counter-GOTV response in supporter areas.

findings.topic: Israel 2015: Netanyahu's election-day 'Arab voters in droves' message
findings.claim: On 17 March 2015, with turnout still lowish, Netanyahu posted an election-day video warning that Arab voters were heading to the polls in large numbers. Testimony in Case 4000 indicates it was pushed by text message to about 700,000 devices in targeted areas, including Likud-heavy neighbourhoods, and a Likud official later said the aim was to raise Jewish turnout. Likud finished well ahead of the final polls (30 seats vs 24 for the Zionist Union). However, no rigorous causal estimate of the video's effect on turnout or vote share was found.
findings.quant: Reach about 700,000 devices (trial testimony). No credible causal effect estimate located.
findings.authors: Wikipedia contributors (citing Israeli press and Case 4000 testimony)
findings.title: Arab voters are streaming in quantity to the polling stations
findings.relevance: Netanyahu's camp has a proven playbook of last-minute, threat-framed SMS and video mobilisation. The model should allow for a late Netanyahu-bloc turnout surge in its strongholds and should not assume symmetrical mobilisation. Its size is unknown, so treat it as a scenario input.

findings.topic: Distance to the polling station and turnout
findings.claim: Using precinct boundaries as natural experiments in Massachusetts and Minnesota, where voting was essentially in person at an assigned polling place, the study finds that a longer trip to the polling place lowers turnout. In non-presidential elections the effect was about three times larger in high-minority areas.
findings.quant: A 1 SD (0.245 mile) increase in distance cut ballots cast by 2-5% across four elections. Earlier-version counterfactual: removing distance effects would add 1.6-4 pp turnout.
findings.authors: Enrico Cantoni
findings.title: A Precinct Too Far: Turnout and Voting Costs
findings.relevance: Israel requires in-person voting at the polling station assigned to one's registered address. Voters registered far from where they live, such as students and young adults registered at their parents' address, face high costs. Election-day logistics and help with travel home have a plausible but unproven effect, so treat this as a separate turnout-potential factor at locality level.

findings.topic: Government GOTV letters to first-time voters (Denmark)
findings.claim: More than 60,000 first-time voters in a Danish election were sent personal letters encouraging them to vote. The letters had small positive effects on validated turnout, little difference between letter versions, and mostly mobilised low-propensity voters, which narrowed participation inequality.
findings.quant: Small positive effects (exact magnitudes not extracted); N over 60,000 first-time voters.
findings.authors: Yosef Bhatti; Jens Olav Dahlgaard; Jonas Hedegaard Hansen; Kasper M. Hansen
findings.title: Can Governments Use Get Out The Vote Letters to Solve Europe's Turnout Crisis? Evidence from a Field Experiment
findings.relevance: In a high-turnout European setting, first-time voters respond to cheap outreach. Supports targeting first-time and young voters (18-22 cohort) in change-bloc-leaning localities with low-cost reminders.

parameters.name: canvass_effect_per_completed_contact_pp
parameters.basis: US high-salience CACE 3.05 (D3-F01). European pooled 0.78 [-0.16, 1.71] vs US 2.50 (D3-F22). Baseline 50-70% gives 1.4-2.1 and 70%+ gives 0.6 (D3-F03). Positive partisan results in Sweden (3.6) and Italy (volunteers 5.0) (D3-F22). Israel = high-salience, PR, about 70% turnout, so take about half of the US high-salience figure.

parameters.name: canvass_baseline_turnout_multiplier
parameters.value: Multiply the base effect by: 1.0 if baseline turnout (individual or locality) <30%; 1.5 if 30-55%; 0.8 if 55-70%; 0.5 if 70-80%; 0.25 if >80%
parameters.basis: Hump-shaped CACE by control turnout: 4.6 / 6.2 / 1.4 / 0.6 (D3-F03). Threshold model in high-salience elections (D3-F18). The European relationship is weaker (D3-F22), so apply softly.

parameters.name: volunteer_phone_effect_per_completed_call_pp
parameters.basis: US high-salience CACE 2.28 (D3-F01). GMA 2013 1.94 (D3-F02). Nickerson 2006 3.8 in low salience (D3-F06). UK evidence that volunteer phones work well (D3-F23). Same approximate halving for Israel.

parameters.name: paid_call_centre_effect_per_completed_call_pp
parameters.basis: US high-salience CACE 0.74 (D3-F01). Low-quality vendors 0.2 vs high-quality 0.9-1.4 (D3-F07).

parameters.name: robocall_effect_itt_pp
parameters.basis: Only low-salience estimates exist (0.58, n=5); not estimable at high salience (D3-F01). Recorded reminders generally ineffective (D3-F07, D3-F11). Israeli voters are saturated with recorded calls at election time.

parameters.name: cold_sms_effect_itt_pp_per_targeted_voter
parameters.basis: US high-salience cold SMS 0.22 [0.05, 0.39] (D3-F01). Green & Gerber 2019 automated texting meta 0.29 (D3-F12). Danish pooled 0.74 in second-order elections (D3-F09). Effect concentrated among casual voters in high-salience races (D3-F08).

parameters.name: warm_sms_effect_itt_pp
parameters.basis: US warm SMS 0.68 [0.05, 1.41] (D3-F01). Dale & Strauss 3.0 among new registrants as an upper anchor (D3-F08).

parameters.name: sms_timing_rule
parameters.value: Send 1-2 messages in the 1-3 days before election day. Weight an election-day-only SMS at 0.7 of a day-before SMS. Extra messages to the same person count 0.
parameters.basis: Danish SMS: pre-election-day messages beat election-day messages; no added effect from multiple messages (D3-F09).

parameters.name: relational_friend_to_friend_effect_per_completed_contact_pp
parameters.basis: Outvote: covariate-adjusted CACE 8.26 [1.18, 15.34], ITT 2.09, even at about 75% baseline turnout (D3-F12). Discounted for a single study, a wide CI and winner's-curse inflation.

parameters.name: standard_gotv_leaflet_mail_itt_pp_per_piece
parameters.basis: High-salience standard mail 0.28; presidential cycles 0.05 (D3-F01). GMA conventional mail 0.16 (D3-F02). Non-advocacy 0.52 in mixed salience (D3-F04). UK leaflet 4.3 is a low-salience outlier (D3-F25). Diminishing returns after about 6 pieces per household.

parameters.name: partisan_advocacy_material_turnout_effect_pp
parameters.basis: Advocacy mail 0.010 [-0.101, 0.120] (D3-F04). Partisan leaflets/mail -0.213 n.s. (D3-F02). Partisan Self mailer null (D3-F05).

parameters.name: social_norm_or_gratitude_message_itt_pp
parameters.basis: High-salience social-pressure mail 1.38 (D3-F01). Gratitude mailers 2.4-2.5 in US low/mid salience. Partisan versions null and vote-history disclosure may not be available in Israel (D3-F05).

parameters.name: email_and_paid_digital_ads_turnout_effect_pp
parameters.basis: Email null (58.7% vs 59.7%). Facebook ads null in two large RCTs. Only a non-purchasable social banner gave 0.39 (D3-F11).

parameters.name: polling_station_festival_effect_pp
parameters.basis: US local-election festivals: +6.5 pp at a 50% baseline, +2.6 at 10%, about $28 per vote (D3-F13). Heavily discounted for a high-salience national election and Israeli rules on activity near polling stations.

parameters.name: vote_plan_script_addon_pp
parameters.value: +1.0 on top of live-contact effect (+2.0 in single-voter households)
parameters.basis: Plan-making ATT 4.1 vs standard -0.2; single-voter households 9.1, multi-voter about 0 (D3-F14). Mixed replications: mail 0.5, one phone null.

parameters.name: household_spillover_ratio
parameters.value: 0.5 for face-to-face / live conversation; 0.3 for SMS and mail
parameters.basis: Canvassing about 60% (D3-F15). SMS about 30% (D3-F10). Larger with partisan discussion in mixed households (D3-F17).

parameters.name: cross_household_neighbourhood_spillover
parameters.basis: No detectable spillover across households (D3-F16). Spillover to parents living elsewhere about 0 (D3-F10).

parameters.name: max_cumulative_turnout_lift_per_targeted_person_pp
parameters.basis: Saturation ground campaign: about +7 pp in the most targeted states, >10 pp in targeted subgroups; effects of multiple contacts roughly additive (D3-F21). Cumulative, non-synergistic effects in England (D3-F24).

parameters.name: contact_rates_for_attempts
parameters.value: Canvass 0.25; volunteer phone 0.12; paid phone 0.10; SMS delivery 0.90
parameters.range: Canvass 0.15-0.40; volunteer phone 0.06-0.25; paid phone 0.05-0.25; SMS 0.80-0.95
parameters.basis: Practitioner contact rates: canvass 25-30%, volunteer phones 10-12%, professional phones about 6% in 2018 (D3-F01). Nickerson & Rogers phone contact 23-26% (D3-F14). Over 90% text delivery (D3-F12). Israeli rates unknown, especially behind building intercoms.

parameters.name: gotv_timing_weight_by_days_before_election
parameters.basis: Final-week calls effective, earlier calls null (Nickerson 2007, D3-F07). Pre-election-day SMS better (D3-F09). Early calls can work in low salience (D3-F29). Persuasion decays (D3-F27). With 16 days left, almost all remaining effort falls in the 1.0 or 0.6 bands.

parameters.name: persuasion_vote_choice_effect_per_completed_conversation_pp
parameters.basis: Zero average in US general elections (D3-F27). +3.2 pp precinct vote share from novel canvassing in multiparty France (D3-F26). Israeli multiparty, within-bloc switching does not change bloc totals.

parameters.name: non_US_discount_on_personal_contact_effects
parameters.basis: European canvassing 0.78 vs US 2.50 (D3-F22). French turnout null (D3-F26). Some positive UK and Swedish results (D3-F23, D3-F25).

parameters.name: counter_mobilisation_penalty
parameters.value: For publicly visible, broadcast-style activity in or about opposing-bloc strongholds, or outgroup-turnout narratives: subtract 0.25 x own gross vote gain as opposing-bloc votes. For targeted private contact with identified supporters: 0.
parameters.basis: Racial-threat proximity effects >10 pp (D3-F31). Israel 2019 backlash: Arab turnout 49% to 59% after the camera campaign (D3-F32). Netanyahu's 2015 election-day threat message (D3-F33). Differential mobilisation in UK partisan experiments (D3-F25). Low-confidence judgement.

parameters.name: messenger_multiplier
parameters.value: Volunteer or co-ethnic/in-language community messenger 1.0; candidate at the door 0.3; commercial vendor 0.4; friend or family member 2.0
parameters.basis: Italy: volunteers CACE 5.0 vs candidates -0.4 (D3-F22). Co-ethnic, in-language contact is effective (D3-F20). Commercial quality gap (D3-F07). Relational effects (D3-F12).

parameters.name: reference_cost_per_net_vote_usd_legacy
parameters.value: Canvass about $19-32; volunteer phone about $26-35; leaflets $23-47; direct mail about $67-69; festivals about $28
parameters.range: Order-of-magnitude only; re-cost for Israeli 2026 labour
parameters.basis: Nickerson 2006 cost comparisons (D3-F06). Festival cost (D3-F13). Pakistan $2.3-3.1 per vote in a low-cost setting (D3-F28).

open_questions: No randomised GOTV experiment from an Israeli Knesset election was found. Every per-contact parameter is carried over from US or European evidence. Can the campaign randomise a share of its door, phone and SMS lists (or whole polling stations, as Pons did) and measure results with official polling-station returns, to calibrate during or after 2026?

Contact rates for Israeli door-knocking (apartment blocks, intercoms, the 2026 security climate) and for phone and SMS lists are unknown. Field data from the campaign's own canvass records are needed.

Social-pressure tactics depend on individual vote histories. It is unclear what Israeli parties may lawfully use; election-day 'who has voted' tracking by party observers is distinct from pre-election vote-history files. Legal review is needed before any social-pressure or 'you voted last time' messaging.

The Knesset Elections Law and party-finance rules may restrict election-day transport, gifts or festivals near polling stations. This needs checking before modelling transport help for voters registered far away (students, young adults, people in the north and south still displaced) or polling-station events.

How big would counter-mobilisation be in Israel? No credible causal estimate exists for the 2015 'droves' video, and the 2019 jump in Arab turnout is confounded by the Joint List's reunification. Locality-level analysis of 2015/2019 turnout shifts in polling-station data held from other desks could give a rough estimate.

Within-bloc mobilisation vs bloc totals: GOTV that moves votes between Yashar, Together, the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu does not change bloc seats. The model needs per-list support shares by locality to convert turnout gains into bloc seats under Bader-Ofer with surplus agreements.

How responsive are Arab localities to outreach by Hebrew-speaking change-bloc campaigners, given that Arab turnout affects whether the Netanyahu bloc reaches 61 even though Arab lists are not part of the change bloc? The messenger-matching evidence (García Bedolla & Michelson) suggests outreach by in-community intermediaries rather than direct change-bloc canvassing.
Is the Outvote relational-texting effect (CACE 8.3) reproducible at scale in Israel's dense WhatsApp-based networks? A quick internal A/B test of relational asks among volunteers is advisable.

Could not verify (search budget exhausted): published DOI of Enos & Fowler (PSRM) and of the Gerber & Green Handbook chapter; Gerber, Gimpel, Green & Shaw (2011) on decay of TV-ad persuasion; Japanese, Irish and Italian (Kendall, Nannicini & Trebbi) GOTV experiments; and a 2023 Electoral Studies study of Brazilian fare-free election-day transit (listed on IPEA's site, reportedly a precise null on turnout despite 7-17% higher ridership), whose page could not be opened.
